description: Hi, I'm Ion, and I am passionate about space exploration. I think the next step of human evolution leads us to explore the worlds outside of our own. I'm looking for members that have original ideas, and who can pitch, but I'm happy for any new members
summary:
Planet Maps is a web app for Moon and Mars mission planning, built by the team “Planet’s Have Feelings Too” (Ion Gumeni, Francesca Olea, Alina Schulz, Tobias Kern) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It uses only open data from NASA and partner agencies.

Its main job is finding Earth analogs. Pick any spot on the Moon or Mars, and the app searches about 96,000 land areas on Earth for the most similar environments. You can weight each parameter, filter by country and limit the search to sites that aren’t known analogs yet. Each result gets a report card showing what matches and what doesn’t, plus estimates of the cost, equipment and people needed to recreate the missing conditions there. The same search finds similar places on the same body.

Colour-coded maps show the data for all three bodies in four projections. Selecting an area lists its parameters, such as slope or temperature variation. On the Moon and Mars, the route planner finds paths from A to B based on terrain, hazards, resources and rover type. Any point can be viewed in 3D, with adjustable time to show the sun’s position. There is also a ruler and a tutorial.
details:
What it does and how it works

Before astronauts and rovers go to the Moon or Mars, they train and test on Earth at "analog" sites that resemble the target. Today those sites are chosen from expert knowledge of a few famous places, such as the Atacama desert, the McMurdo Dry Valleys and Iceland. Planet Maps makes that choice data-driven.

You pick any spot on the Moon or Mars and set a radius of 1 to 250 km. The app then compares that area with about 96,000 land areas on Earth, using open NASA data for all three worlds. It compares temperatures (maximum, minimum, day–night swing), slope, relief, dryness and rain, sunlight, bare ground, frozen ground and dust. Each Earth place gets a percentage match and a report card that marks every characteristic as strong, partial or weak. Values beyond anything on Earth, such as Moon temperatures of +122 °C and −178 °C, are matched by rank only, and the card says so.

Around this search the app offers:

  • Simulation Planning: for a chosen analog, it lists what it would take to recreate the missing conditions there: the environmental gaps, recommended equipment (for example a thermal vacuum chamber, a Mars atmosphere chamber, regolith simulant or UV lamps), cost ranges labelled as published or estimated, the team and the timeline, with sources.
  • Site finder: it searches a whole body by criteria, with presets such as "Safe landing", "Water ice within reach" and "South pole sunlight" (Artemis). With "Safe landing", 8.7% of Mars meets every limit, and the best area is in Elysium Planitia, the plain where InSight landed.
  • Route planner: on Mars and the Moon it gives safest, easiest, shortest and energy-efficient routes. It respects slope limits of 20° on foot (NASA xEVA spec) and 25° for a rover, and has profiles for NASA's five Mars rovers and the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle. A route can be replayed at its Earth analog for a side-by-side comparison.
  • Maps and data layers: colour-coded data layers in four projections, area summaries, reverse search (from Earth to Mars or the Moon), a search for similar spots on the same body, 3D terrain with adjustable sun position, a ruler and a tutorial.

Benefits

The app widens the search from a handful of known sites to every land area on Earth. It is honest about each match, so mission teams see what a site can test and what it can't. It also connects a site to practical planning: landing, driving, navigation and the equipment needed to close the gaps.

Intended impact

We want mission planners, researchers and students to find new, well-characterized analogs quickly. Our results show it works. For six Moon and Mars sites with an established Earth analog, the known analog ranked above a random place on Earth for five of them, and three of those ranked in the top 5% of all areas. Across 20 sites and 10 results each, 94% of results were more than 250 km from any of 25 established analog sites. Examples include the Apollo 11 landing plain with the Borkou plains in Chad (93% match), Gale crater with Isabela Island in the Galápagos (85%), and Valles Marineris with the Karakoram in Pakistan (81%). None of these is an established analog site.

Tools and software

We used JavaScript, Vite, Leaflet for the maps, three.js for the 3D globes and terrain, and Web Workers for the search. The app is hosted on GitHub Pages and runs in any browser without installation. All data is open, from NASA and partner agencies.

Creativity

Most analog work starts from a place on Earth and asks what it resembles. We turned it around: start from the target on the Moon or Mars and search the whole planet. The report card shows where an analogy breaks down, not just where it holds. Simulation Planning and the route replay then turn a match into a test plan.

Factors we considered

Earth cannot reproduce everything. No place on Earth has 1/6 or 3/8 gravity, vacuum or Mars's thin CO₂ air (0.6% of Earth's pressure), the radiation (Curiosity measured about 0.7 mSv a day), the Moon's two-week days and nights, Mars's perchlorate soil, or sterility. The app does not yet compare rock type and minerals, impact craters are shown but not scored, and the Earth search grid is 0.5° (about 50 km). We state these limits in the app instead of hiding them.
